# Work, Jobs, and Leadership {#work-leadership}

Beginning in late 2010, a large Chinese travel agency ran an unusual experiment. Call-centre
employees who volunteered to work from home were randomly assigned either to do so
or to stay in the office. The home workers became more productive and quit less
often, yet a large share of them later chose to come back to the office, citing
isolation [@bloom2015]. Around the same time, managers everywhere were asking
related questions. Why does one team thrive under a demanding manager while
another burns out? Why do employees accept a pay cut with grace in one plant and
retaliate in another? Why is the chief executive paid several times more than the
vice presidents who report to her, even when their jobs look similar?

These puzzles share a theme: the *design* of work and of the relationships around
it shapes what people do, feel, and contribute. This chapter assembles the
theories that organizational psychologists and personnel economists use to
explain those effects. We start with the **job** itself (the job characteristics
model, [job demands-resources theory](#job-demands-resources), [conservation of resources theory](#conservation-of-resources), and
[affective events theory](#affective-events-theory)). We then turn to **leadership** ([leader-member exchange](#leader-member-exchange),
[transformational leadership](#transformational-leadership), and [path-goal theory](#path-goal-theory)) and to the **employment
relationship** (psychological contracts, [organizational justice](#organizational-justice), organizational
commitment, and [person-environment fit](#person-environment-fit)). We close with two economic theories of
**investment and rewards**: [human capital theory](#human-capital-theory) and [tournament theory](#tournament-theory). Together
they form the analytical core of human resource management, people analytics, and
leadership development (Table \@ref(tab:tab-wl-glance)).

```{r tab-wl-glance}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Theory, ~`Core question`, ~`Level of analysis`, ~`Key source`,
  "Job characteristics model", "Which features of a job make it motivating?", "Individual / job", "Hackman & Oldham (1976)",
  "Job demands-resources", "What drives burnout and engagement?", "Individual / job", "Demerouti et al. (2001)",
  "Conservation of resources", "Why is resource loss so stressful?", "Individual", "Hobfoll (1989)",
  "Affective events theory", "How do daily events shape feelings and behaviour at work?", "Individual (within person)", "Weiss & Cropanzano (1996)",
  "Leader-member exchange", "Why do leaders build different relationships with different followers?", "Dyad", "Graen & Uhl-Bien (1995)",
  "Transformational leadership", "How do leaders inspire performance beyond expectations?", "Individual / group", "Bass (1985)",
  "Path-goal theory", "Which leader behaviour fits which situation?", "Dyad / group", "House (1971)",
  "Psychological contract", "What do employees believe they were promised?", "Individual / dyad", "Rousseau (1989)",
  "Organizational justice", "When do people judge decisions and treatment as fair?", "Individual / organization", "Colquitt et al. (2001)",
  "Organizational commitment", "What binds employees to an organization?", "Individual", "Meyer & Allen (1991)",
  "Person-environment fit", "Does the match between person and setting matter?", "Individual / organization", "Kristof (1996)",
  "Human capital theory", "Who should pay for skills, and which skills?", "Individual / firm", "Becker (1964)",
  "Tournament theory", "Why do pay gaps widen up the hierarchy?", "Firm / labour market", "Lazear & Rosen (1981)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Chapter at a glance: theories of work, jobs, and leadership.")
```

## Job Characteristics Model {#job-characteristics-model}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Jobs that offer skill variety, task identity, task significance,
autonomy, and feedback produce three critical psychological states, and these
states raise internal work motivation, satisfaction, and performance, especially
for people who want to grow at work.

**Origins.** Organizational psychology. @hackman1975 developed the Job Diagnostic
Survey, @hackman1976 stated and tested the model, and @hackman1980 applied it to
the practice of work redesign.

**Level of analysis.** The individual job holder and the job.

**Key constructs.** Core job dimensions, experienced meaningfulness, experienced
responsibility, knowledge of results, internal work motivation, growth need
strength, motivating potential score.

**Boundary conditions.** Strongest for employees with high growth need strength
and adequate knowledge and skill. Weaker when pay, security, or supervision are
so poor that they dominate attention.

**Related theories.** [Self-determination theory](#self-determination-theory) (Section \@ref(self-determination-theory)),
[Job demands-resources](#job-demands-resources),
[Goal-setting theory](#goal-setting-theory) (Section \@ref(goal-setting-theory)),
[Social information processing](#social-information-processing) (Section \@ref(social-information-processing)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Twentieth-century industrial engineering had a clear answer to the question of
how to design a job: break it into the smallest possible units, standardise them,
and remove discretion. The assembly line embodied this logic and delivered large
productivity gains, but it also delivered boredom, absenteeism, and turnover.
Herzberg's two-factor theory [@herzberg1959] and the human relations movement had
already argued that the content of work matters for motivation. What was missing
was a precise, measurable account of *which* job features matter and *why*.

@hackman1975 supplied the measure, the Job Diagnostic Survey (JDS), and
@hackman1976 supplied the theory. Their model specified a small set of objective
job features, a set of psychological states through which those features work, and
an individual difference that conditions the whole chain. The resulting **job
characteristics model** (JCM) became the dominant framework for job design for
three decades and remains the starting point for modern work design research
[@parker2014].

### Core logic and propositions

The model links five **core job dimensions** to three **critical psychological
states** (Table \@ref(tab:tab-wl-jcm)). **Skill variety**, **task identity**
(completing a whole, identifiable piece of work), and **task significance**
(impact on other people) jointly create **experienced meaningfulness**.
**Autonomy** creates **experienced responsibility** for outcomes. **Feedback**
from the job itself creates **knowledge of results**. When all three states are
present, people feel good when they perform well, and this self-generated reward
sustains **internal work motivation** [@hackman1976].

```{r tab-wl-jcm}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Core dimension`, ~Definition, ~`Psychological state`, ~`Low-scoring example`, ~`Redesign lever`,
  "Skill variety", "Range of activities and skills the job requires", "Meaningfulness", "Single repetitive assembly step", "Job enlargement, rotation",
  "Task identity", "Completing a whole, visible piece of work", "Meaningfulness", "Processing one field of a form", "Natural work units, case ownership",
  "Task significance", "Impact of the work on other people", "Meaningfulness", "Back-office task with no visible user", "Contact with beneficiaries",
  "Autonomy", "Discretion over scheduling and methods", "Responsibility", "Scripted call handling", "Vertical loading, self-managing teams",
  "Feedback", "Direct information about performance from the work itself", "Knowledge of results", "Quality checked by a later department", "Open feedback channels, dashboards"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "The five core job dimensions of the job characteristics model and how they can be redesigned.")
```

The original propositions can be stated as follows:

- **P1 (Dimensions to states).** Variety, identity, and significance raise
  experienced meaningfulness. Autonomy raises experienced responsibility.
  Feedback raises knowledge of results.
- **P2 (States to outcomes).** The three states jointly raise internal motivation,
  growth satisfaction, general satisfaction, and work quality, and reduce
  absenteeism and turnover.
- **P3 (Moderation).** These relationships are stronger for employees high in
  **growth need strength**, the desire for challenge and personal development. In
  the later formulation, knowledge and skill and satisfaction with the work
  context were added as moderators [@hackman1980].

Because the model argues that all three psychological states must be present,
Hackman and Oldham proposed a **motivating potential score** (MPS) that combines
the dimensions multiplicatively:

$$
\text{MPS} = \frac{\text{Skill variety} + \text{Task identity} + \text{Task significance}}{3}
\times \text{Autonomy} \times \text{Feedback}
$$

The formula averages the three meaningfulness dimensions, so a weakness in one can
be offset by strength in another, but it multiplies autonomy and feedback, so a
job with no autonomy or no feedback has a motivating potential close to zero no
matter how varied it is.

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wl-jcm) shows the job characteristics model.

```{r fig-wl-jcm, fig.cap = "The job characteristics model. Core job dimensions create critical psychological states that drive motivation and performance. Growth need strength, knowledge and skill, and context satisfaction moderate the chain. Adapted from Hackman and Oldham (1976, 1980)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  V [label = "Skill variety\\nTask identity\\nTask significance", %s]
  A [label = "Autonomy", %s]
  F [label = "Feedback", %s]
  M [label = "Experienced\\nmeaningfulness", %s]
  R [label = "Experienced\\nresponsibility", %s]
  K [label = "Knowledge of\\nresults", %s]
  O [label = "Internal motivation\\nSatisfaction\\nWork quality\\nLower turnover", %s]
  G [label = "Growth need strength\\nKnowledge and skill\\nContext satisfaction", %s]
  V -> M
  A -> R
  F -> K
  M -> O
  R -> O
  K -> O
  G -> O [style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism,
   node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wl-mps) shows why the multiplicative formula matters.
Consider four stylised jobs. The additive index (the simple mean of the five
dimensions) ranks the scripted call-centre job as moderately enriched because it
scores well on feedback and significance. The MPS ranks it near the bottom
because autonomy is almost absent. Whether the multiplicative form is correct is
an empirical question, and the evidence on it is discussed below.

```{r fig-wl-mps, fig.cap = "Illustrative comparison of the multiplicative motivating potential score (MPS) and a simple additive index for four stylised jobs. Both indices are rescaled to a 0-100 range. Jobs that lack autonomy are penalised far more heavily by the MPS. Stylised scores, not empirical data.", fig.height = 3.8}
jobs <- tibble::tribble(
  ~job, ~variety, ~identity, ~significance, ~autonomy, ~feedback,
  "Assembly-line operator", 2, 2, 3, 1.5, 4,
  "Scripted call-centre agent", 3, 4, 5, 1.2, 6,
  "Field service technician", 5, 6, 5, 5.5, 5,
  "Product designer", 6.5, 5, 5.5, 6, 4.5
)
jobs <- jobs |>
  mutate(mps = (variety + identity + significance) / 3 * autonomy * feedback,
         additive = (variety + identity + significance + autonomy + feedback) / 5,
         `MPS (multiplicative)` = 100 * mps / 343,
         `Additive index` = 100 * (additive - 1) / 6) |>
  select(job, `MPS (multiplicative)`, `Additive index`) |>
  pivot_longer(-job, names_to = "index", values_to = "score") |>
  mutate(job = factor(job, levels = rev(c("Assembly-line operator", "Scripted call-centre agent",
                                          "Field service technician", "Product designer"))))
ggplot(jobs, aes(score, job, fill = index)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(score)), position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            hjust = -0.2, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("MPS (multiplicative)" = pal[["blue"]], "Additive index" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Motivating potential (rescaled, 0-100)", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       title = "Autonomy and feedback act as multipliers in the MPS",
       caption = "Stylised: dimensions scored 1-7. MPS divided by its maximum (343). Additive index is the mean of the five dimensions.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The JCM generated hundreds of studies. An early meta-analysis found reasonable
support for links between the core dimensions and psychological outcomes such as
satisfaction and internal motivation, weaker links to behavioural outcomes such as
performance and absenteeism, and little advantage for the multiplicative MPS over
simpler additive combinations [@fried1987]. The psychological states received
partial support as mediators.

The most comprehensive later synthesis, by @humphrey2007, broadened the model in
two ways. First, it confirmed that the motivational characteristics of the JCM
relate to satisfaction, motivation, and performance, with experienced
meaningfulness carrying much of the effect. Second, it showed that **social
characteristics** (interdependence, social support, feedback from others) and
**work context** explain additional variance in attitudes beyond the classic five
dimensions. The Work Design Questionnaire was developed to measure this wider set
of task, knowledge, social, and contextual features [@morgeson2006].

Two further extensions changed how the field thinks about jobs. @grant2008 showed
experimentally that connecting employees with the people who benefit from their
work, for instance letting fundraising callers learn how scholarships changed
recipients' lives, raised persistence and performance. This made **task
significance** a relational, designable feature rather than a fixed property of a
job. @wrzesniewski2001 introduced **job crafting**, the idea that employees
actively reshape the task, relational, and cognitive boundaries of their own jobs.
Work design is therefore not only something managers do to employees. It is also
something employees do for themselves [@parker2014].

::: {.debate}
**How objective are job characteristics?** The JCM treats job characteristics as
features of the work, but most studies measure them with incumbents' perceptions
gathered in the same survey as satisfaction and motivation. Critics in the
[social information processing](#social-information-processing) (Section \@ref(social-information-processing)) tradition argued
that perceptions of a job are partly constructed from coworkers' cues, and that
satisfied workers may simply describe their jobs more favourably. Common-method
variance therefore inflates many correlations. Studies that use independent
raters, objective job data (such as occupational databases), or field
experiments that change jobs provide more credible estimates, and those effects
are generally smaller, especially for performance. A second dispute concerns the
MPS itself: the evidence offers little reason to prefer the multiplicative formula
to a simple average [@fried1987].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Job redesign on the assembly line.** In 1974 Volvo opened an assembly plant at
Kalmar, Sweden, organised around work teams that assembled larger portions of each
car instead of performing short, repetitive cycles on a conventional moving line.
The design applied JCM principles directly: larger work units raised task identity
and variety, and team responsibility for scheduling and quality raised autonomy.
Volvo later went further at its Uddevalla plant. Both plants were closed in the
1990s, and analysts still disagree about whether their productivity record
vindicated or undermined the approach. The lasting lesson is that enrichment
interacts with technology and volume: the same design that motivates in
low-volume, high-variety production may be uneconomic on a high-volume line.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: redesigning a claims-processing unit.** An insurer
organises claims processing by function: one clerk verifies policy data, another
assesses damage, a third approves payment. Customers wait, and clerks report low
motivation. A JCM-based redesign assigns each adjuster a portfolio of whole claims
(task identity), gives authority to approve payments below a threshold (autonomy),
and shows each adjuster weekly data on cycle time and customer ratings for their
own cases (feedback). The model predicts the largest gains among adjusters high in
growth need strength, and it warns that adjusters lacking assessment skills will
experience the redesign as overload. Training must therefore precede enrichment.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Autonomy is positively related to proactive behaviour, and the
  relationship is mediated by experienced responsibility.
- *H2.* The positive effect of task significance on performance is stronger when
  employees have direct contact with beneficiaries.
- *H3.* Job enrichment raises internal motivation more for employees high in
  growth need strength than for those low in growth need strength.

**Validated scales.** Job Diagnostic Survey [@hackman1975]. Work Design
Questionnaire covering task, knowledge, social, and contextual characteristics
[@morgeson2006].

**Designs.** Field experiments or quasi-experiments around job redesign
programmes. Multi-source designs pairing incumbent reports with supervisor or
expert ratings of job features. Linking occupational databases to employee survey
or administrative outcome data. Diary studies of job crafting.

**Contexts.** Call centres, healthcare, manufacturing teams, platform and gig
work, algorithmically managed jobs.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Treating perceived job characteristics as objective causes.** When job features,
motivation, and satisfaction come from the same respondent at the same time, a
correlation between them says little about the effect of redesign. Use
independent sources for job characteristics, exploit changes in jobs over time,
and be cautious about the MPS, which adds measurement error without clear
predictive gain.
:::

## Job Demands-Resources Theory {#job-demands-resources}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Every job has demands that cost energy and resources that help
achieve goals. High demands drive a health-impairment process that leads to
burnout, and plentiful resources drive a motivational process that leads to
engagement. Resources also buffer the strain caused by demands.

**Origins.** Occupational health psychology. @demerouti2001 introduced the model
as an account of burnout. @bakker2007 extended it to engagement, and @bakker2017
restated it as a theory.

**Level of analysis.** Individual employee within a job, increasingly studied at
team and day level.

**Key constructs.** Job demands, job resources, personal resources, exhaustion,
disengagement, burnout, work engagement, buffering, job crafting.

**Boundary conditions.** Demands and resources are defined by their function, so
the same feature (for example, time pressure) may act as a challenge in one
setting and a hindrance in another.

**Related theories.** [Job characteristics model](#job-characteristics-model),
[Conservation of resources](#conservation-of-resources),
[Self-determination theory](#self-determination-theory) (Section \@ref(self-determination-theory)),
[Broaden-and-build theory](#broaden-and-build-theory) (Section \@ref(broaden-and-build-theory)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Before JD-R, two research traditions dominated the study of job stress. The
**demand-control model** argued that strain arises when high job demands meet low
decision latitude [@karasek1979]. Burnout research, led by Christina Maslach,
described a syndrome of exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced efficacy common in
human-service jobs [@maslach2001]. Both traditions were productive but narrow:
they named only a few demands and a single resource (control), and they focused on
ill health rather than on positive states.

@demerouti2001 proposed a more general model. Any job, they argued, can be
described with two broad categories. **Job demands** are physical, psychological,
social, or organizational aspects of the job that require sustained effort and
therefore carry physiological or psychological costs. **Job resources** are aspects
that help achieve work goals, reduce demands and their costs, or stimulate growth.
In their study, demands were primarily related to exhaustion, while a lack of
resources was primarily related to disengagement. The generality of the model,
which lets researchers choose the demands and resources relevant to a given
occupation, is a major reason for its spread.

### Core logic and propositions

@bakker2007 and @bakker2017 summarise the theory in a small set of propositions:

- **P1 (Two categories).** Job characteristics can be classified as demands or
  resources.
- **P2 (Health impairment).** Chronic high demands exhaust mental and physical
  energy and lead to burnout and health problems.
- **P3 (Motivation).** Job resources foster work engagement and, through it,
  performance and retention.
- **P4 (Buffering).** Resources weaken the effect of demands on strain.
- **P5 (Boosting).** Resources matter most for motivation when demands are high,
  because resources become salient when they are needed to cope.
- **P6 (Personal resources and crafting).** Optimism, [self-efficacy](#social-cognitive-theory) (Section \@ref(social-cognitive-theory)), and similar
  personal resources work like job resources. Engaged employees craft their jobs
  to gain resources, while exhausted employees may undermine themselves and create
  more demands, producing reciprocal spirals.

@schaufeli2004 tested the [dual-process](#dual-process-theory) (Section \@ref(dual-process-theory)) structure with structural equation models
in several samples: burnout mediated the link between demands and health problems,
and engagement mediated the link between resources and turnover intentions (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wl-jdr)).

```{r fig-wl-jdr, fig.cap = "The dual processes of job demands-resources theory. Demands drive burnout through a health-impairment process. Resources drive engagement through a motivational process. Dashed arrows show buffering and the reciprocal effect of engagement on resources through job crafting. Adapted from Bakker and Demerouti (2007, 2017)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  D  [label = "Job demands\\n(workload, emotional\\ndemands, role conflict)", %s]
  R  [label = "Job resources\\n(autonomy, support,\\nfeedback, development)", %s]
  B  [label = "Burnout\\n(exhaustion,\\ncynicism)", %s]
  E  [label = "Work engagement\\n(vigour, dedication,\\nabsorption)", %s]
  H  [label = "Health problems\\nAbsence", %s]
  P  [label = "Performance\\nRetention", %s]
  D -> B [label = " health\\n impairment"]
  R -> E [label = " motivation"]
  B -> H
  E -> P
  B -> P [label = " (-)"]
  R -> B [style = dashed, label = " buffers"]
  E -> R [style = dashed, label = " job crafting", constraint = false]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_outcome))
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wl-jdr-sim) illustrates the buffering proposition with
simulated data. Burnout rises with demands for everyone, but the slope is much
steeper for employees with few resources.

```{r fig-wl-jdr-sim, fig.cap = "Illustrative simulation of the buffering hypothesis. Burnout rises with job demands, but the slope is flatter for employees with high job resources. Simulated data, not empirical estimates.", fig.height = 4}
set.seed(2001)
n <- 1200
jdr <- tibble(
  demands = runif(n, 1, 7),
  resources = runif(n, 1, 7)
) |>
  mutate(burnout = 3 + 0.55 * (demands - 4) - 0.45 * (resources - 4) -
           0.10 * (demands - 4) * (resources - 4) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.6),
         group = ifelse(resources >= 4, "High job resources", "Low job resources"))
ggplot(jdr, aes(demands, burnout, colour = group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.18, size = 1.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Low job resources" = pal[["orange"]], "High job resources" = pal[["blue"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
  labs(x = "Job demands (1-7)", y = "Burnout (simulated score)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Resources buffer the strain caused by demands",
       caption = "Stylised simulation (n = 1,200) with a negative demands x resources interaction.")
```

Table \@ref(tab:tab-wl-jdr) lists typical demands and resources studied in
different occupations, which shows how the model's open-ended categories are
adapted to context.

```{r tab-wl-jdr}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Occupation, ~`Typical job demands`, ~`Typical job resources`, ~`Likely outcome if unbalanced`,
  "Nursing", "Emotional demands, shift work, patient load", "Team support, autonomy in care decisions", "Exhaustion, absence, exit from profession",
  "Software engineering", "Deadline pressure, on-call interruptions", "Autonomy, learning opportunities, clear priorities", "Cynicism, reduced code quality",
  "Retail and hospitality", "Customer hostility, emotional labour, irregular hours", "Supervisor support, predictable scheduling", "Turnover, service failures",
  "Teaching", "Classroom disruption, administrative load", "Collegial support, professional discretion", "Burnout, early career exit",
  "Remote knowledge work", "Blurred boundaries, communication overload", "Schedule control, manager check-ins, peer contact", "Isolation, overwork"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Examples of job demands and resources across occupations. Categories are illustrative and must be tailored in each study.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The dual-process structure is well supported across countries and occupations
[@schaufeli2004; @bakker2017]. The most important refinement concerns demands.
@lepine2005 distinguished **challenge stressors** (workload, responsibility, time
urgency) from **hindrance stressors** (red tape, role ambiguity, politics) and
showed meta-analytically that challenge stressors relate positively to motivation
and performance while hindrance stressors relate negatively. @crawford2010
integrated this distinction into JD-R: challenge demands were positively related
to engagement, hindrance demands negatively, and both were positively related to
burnout. A job can therefore be both energising and exhausting.

Evidence on the interaction propositions is more mixed. Buffering and boosting
effects appear in many studies, but they are typically small and are sensitive to
how demands and resources are matched. Day-level diary studies show that
engagement and exhaustion fluctuate within persons, which has moved JD-R toward
dynamic, within-person tests [@bakker2017].

::: {.debate}
**Is JD-R a theory or a heuristic?** Because almost any job feature can be labelled
a demand or a resource, critics argue that JD-R is too flexible to be falsified:
a feature that predicts burnout becomes a demand, one that predicts engagement
becomes a resource. The challenge-hindrance distinction sharpens predictions but
also concedes that the same feature can play either role. Defenders reply that
the theory specifies distinct processes, mediators, and interactions that can
fail empirically, and that @bakker2017 added reciprocal and personal-resource
propositions that are testable. Researchers should therefore classify demands and
resources *before* seeing the data and justify the classification from the
occupation's work processes.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Burnout and remote work (conceptual application).** Remote and hybrid work
change both sides of the JD-R ledger. They typically add resources, notably
schedule control and fewer commuting demands, and meta-analytic evidence links
telecommuting to higher perceived autonomy and lower work-family conflict
[@gajendran2007]. They can also remove resources (informal peer support,
spontaneous feedback) and add demands (communication overload, blurred boundaries
between work and home). The randomized experiment at the travel agency described in
the chapter opening illustrates both sides: home work raised performance and
reduced quits, but isolation led many employees to return [@bloom2015]. A JD-R
audit of a hybrid policy therefore asks which resources are lost when people are
apart and how to replace them (structured check-ins, team days, clear
availability norms), rather than treating remote work as uniformly good or bad.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: an engagement survey that measures the wrong thing.** A
retailer's annual engagement survey shows falling scores in distribution centres.
Leadership responds with recognition programmes, a pure resource intervention.
A JD-R diagnosis separates demands from resources and finds the real driver: a new
scheduling algorithm that raised unpredictability, a hindrance demand. Resources
cannot fully offset a hindrance demand that is cheap to remove. The more effective
intervention restores advance notice of shifts and only then invests in
recognition.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Workload is positively related to emotional exhaustion, and the
  relationship is weaker for employees who report high supervisor support.
- *H2.* Hindrance demands are negatively related to engagement, whereas challenge
  demands are positively related to engagement.
- *H3.* Day-level engagement predicts next-day job crafting, which in turn
  increases job resources.

**Validated scales.** Maslach Burnout Inventory [@maslach2001]. Oldenburg Burnout
Inventory, which measures exhaustion and disengagement [@demerouti2001]. Utrecht
Work Engagement Scale, short form [@schaufeli2006].

**Designs.** Multi-wave panels with cross-lagged models. Daily diary studies with
multilevel models that separate within-person from between-person effects.
Intervention studies (workload reduction, job crafting training). Linking survey
data to sickness absence and turnover records.

**Contexts.** Healthcare, education, call centres, hybrid work, platform work.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Labelling variables after the fact.** Post hoc classification of a feature as a
demand or resource, chosen to fit the results, makes JD-R unfalsifiable. Specify
classifications in advance, distinguish challenge from hindrance demands, and
test the interaction propositions with adequately powered designs rather than
reporting only main effects.
:::

## Conservation of Resources Theory {#conservation-of-resources}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** People strive to obtain, retain, and protect what they value.
Stress occurs when resources are threatened, lost, or not regained after
investment, and resource loss weighs more heavily than equivalent gain.

**Origins.** Stress psychology. @hobfoll1989, reviewed for organizational research
by @halbesleben2014 and @hobfoll2018.

**Level of analysis.** Individual, with extensions to teams and organizations.

**Key constructs.** Resources (objects, conditions, personal characteristics,
energies), resource loss, resource investment, loss spirals, gain spirals,
resource caravans.

**Boundary conditions.** What counts as a resource depends on a person's goals and
culture, so predictions require careful specification of the resource in
question.

**Related theories.** [Job demands-resources](#job-demands-resources),
[Loss aversion](#loss-aversion) (Section \@ref(loss-aversion)), [Prospect theory](#prospect-theory-model) (Section \@ref(prospect-theory-model)).
:::

@hobfoll1989 proposed conservation of resources (COR) theory as an alternative to
appraisal-based models of stress. He defined resources broadly: **objects**
(a home, tools), **conditions** (tenure, a good marriage), **personal
characteristics** (self-esteem, skills), and **energies** (time, money,
knowledge). Stress follows when these are threatened or lost, or when people
invest resources and fail to obtain a return.

Two principles give the theory its distinctive predictions. The **primacy of
loss** states that resource loss is disproportionately more salient than resource
gain, a parallel to [loss aversion](#loss-aversion) (Section \@ref(loss-aversion)) in decision research. The
**resource investment** principle states that people must invest resources to
protect against loss, recover from it, and gain new resources. From these follow
the corollaries that people with more resources are less vulnerable to loss and
better able to gain, and that loss and gain both tend to cumulate in **spirals**
[@hobfoll2018]. The later formulation also adds a **desperation** principle: when
resources are outstretched or exhausted, people may switch to defensive,
sometimes seemingly irrational, behaviour to preserve what is left (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wl-cor)).

```{r fig-wl-cor, fig.cap = "Illustrative simulation of resource spirals. Employees above a resource threshold tend to accumulate resources (gain spirals), while those below it tend to lose them (loss spirals), because both loss and gain are self-reinforcing. Simulated trajectories, not empirical data.", fig.height = 4}
set.seed(1989)
n_emp <- 40
periods <- 12
start <- seq(2.2, 7.8, length.out = n_emp)
traj <- lapply(seq_len(n_emp), function(i) {
  r <- numeric(periods)
  r[1] <- start[i]
  for (t in 2:periods) {
    r[t] <- r[t - 1] + 0.12 * (r[t - 1] - 5) + rnorm(1, 0, 0.25)
    r[t] <- min(max(r[t], 0), 10)
  }
  tibble(id = i, period = seq_len(periods), resources = r,
         start_group = ifelse(start[i] >= 5, "Started above threshold", "Started below threshold"))
}) |> bind_rows()
ggplot(traj, aes(period, resources, group = id, colour = start_group)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["muted"]]) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.55, linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("label", x = 1, y = 5, label = "Resource threshold", hjust = 0, size = 3.2,
           colour = ink[["secondary"]], fill = ink[["surface"]], label.size = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Started above threshold" = pal[["blue"]], "Started below threshold" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, periods, 2)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 10)) +
  labs(x = "Period", y = "Resource stock (index)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Gain spirals and loss spirals",
       caption = "Stylised: resources change by 0.12 x (distance from threshold) plus noise each period. 40 simulated employees.")
```

COR has become one of the most cited theories in organizational behaviour, used
to explain burnout, work-family conflict, the effects of abusive supervision, and
why employees withhold discretionary effort when they feel depleted
[@halbesleben2014]. Its breadth is also its main weakness. @halbesleben2014
observe that almost anything has been called a resource, and they propose defining
a resource as anything an individual perceives as helping attain his or her goals.
That definition improves coherence but makes resources subjective and
goal-dependent, which complicates measurement.

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: protecting resources during a reorganization.** A bank
merges two operations teams. COR predicts that the threat of losing valued
conditions (a known role, a trusted manager, seniority) will produce stress before
any loss occurs, and that employees who already have fewer resources (new hires,
those caring for family members) will be most vulnerable to a loss spiral. Practical
responses follow from the theory: announce what will *not* change, protect key
resources such as schedule predictability during the transition, and target
support at the employees with the thinnest resource reserves.
:::

## Affective Events Theory {#affective-events-theory}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Discrete events at work trigger emotional reactions. These
reactions drive immediate, affect-driven behaviours and, accumulated over time,
shape attitudes such as job satisfaction, which in turn drive considered,
judgment-driven behaviours.

**Origins.** Organizational psychology. @weiss1996.

**Level of analysis.** Individual, with emphasis on within-person variation over
time.

**Key constructs.** Work environment features, work events (hassles and uplifts),
affective reactions (moods and emotions), affective dispositions, work attitudes,
affect-driven behaviour, judgment-driven behaviour.

**Boundary conditions.** Most useful for explaining short-term fluctuations and
spontaneous behaviours. Less informative for stable, between-person differences
in attitudes.

**Related theories.** [Appraisal theory](#appraisal-theory) (Section \@ref(appraisal-theory)),
[Affect circumplex](#affect-circumplex) (Section \@ref(affect-circumplex)),
[Broaden-and-build theory](#broaden-and-build-theory) (Section \@ref(broaden-and-build-theory)).
:::

For decades, job satisfaction research treated satisfaction as an emotional
state and studied it as a stable, between-person attitude explained by stable
job features. @weiss1996 argued that this conflated two different things. Job
satisfaction is an **evaluative judgment** about one's job. Emotions and moods are
**affective experiences** that occur in response to events, fluctuate within a
day, and have their own consequences. Affective events theory (AET) places the
**event** at the centre of the analysis (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wl-aet)).

```{r fig-wl-aet, fig.cap = "Affective events theory. Features of the work environment make some events more likely. Events trigger affective reactions, moderated by dispositions. Affect drives spontaneous behaviour directly and, through attitudes, judgment-driven behaviour. Adapted from Weiss and Cropanzano (1996)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  W [label = "Work environment\\nfeatures", %s]
  E [label = "Work events\\n(hassles, uplifts)", %s]
  A [label = "Affective reactions\\n(moods, emotions)", %s]
  D [label = "Dispositions\\n(trait affect)", %s]
  S [label = "Work attitudes\\n(job satisfaction)", %s]
  B1 [label = "Affect-driven\\nbehaviour\\n(helping, outbursts)", %s]
  B2 [label = "Judgment-driven\\nbehaviour\\n(quitting decisions)", %s]
  W -> E -> A
  D -> A [style = dashed]
  A -> B1
  A -> S -> B2
  W -> S [style = dotted, label = " cognitive\\n evaluation"]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_moderator, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_outcome))
```

AET makes three contributions. First, it distinguishes **affect-driven
behaviours**, such as helping a colleague in a good mood or snapping at a customer
after an insult, from **judgment-driven behaviours**, such as deciding to quit,
which follow from considered attitudes. Second, it implies that the *pattern* of
events over time, not only the average job, shapes satisfaction. Third, it
requires methods that capture within-person dynamics. @weiss1999 showed that mood
and beliefs about the job independently predict satisfaction, and experience
sampling studies found that a substantial share of the variance in mood and job
satisfaction lies within persons over time [@ilies2002].

::: {.business-case}
**Service work and the management of events.** In front-line service jobs, a small
number of hostile customer interactions can dominate an employee's day. AET
suggests that managers can influence affect by changing the *frequency* of
negative events (better routing of difficult calls, clear escalation paths) and by
providing recovery opportunities after them (short breaks, supervisor debriefs),
not only by improving average pay or job content. Because affect-driven behaviour is
immediate, the timing of support matters: help offered shortly after an incident
prevents spillover into the next customer interaction.
:::

## Leader-Member Exchange {#leader-member-exchange}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Leaders develop relationships of different quality with different
followers. High-quality exchanges, built on trust, respect, and mutual obligation,
lead to better performance, attitudes, and retention than low-quality exchanges
limited to the formal employment contract.

**Origins.** Organizational psychology. The vertical dyad linkage studies of
@dansereau1975, consolidated as leader-member exchange (LMX) theory by
@graen1995.

**Level of analysis.** The leader-follower dyad, with extensions to the
differentiation of relationships within teams.

**Key constructs.** LMX quality, role making, leadership making (stranger,
acquaintance, partnership), LMX differentiation, in-group and out-group.

**Boundary conditions.** Assumes leaders have discretion over resources,
assignments, and latitude. Effects of differentiation depend on whether team
members see it as fair.

**Related theories.** [Social exchange theory](#social-exchange-theory) (Section \@ref(social-exchange-theory)),
[Transformational leadership](#transformational-leadership),
[Organizational justice](#organizational-justice),
[Psychological safety](#psychological-safety) (Section \@ref(psychological-safety)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Most early leadership theories assumed an **average leadership style**: a leader
behaves in roughly the same way toward everyone, and that style can be described by
averaging subordinates' ratings. @dansereau1975 challenged this assumption with a
longitudinal study of managers and their direct reports. They found that managers
formed distinct relationships with different subordinates within the first months:
some became trusted assistants with latitude and influence, others were managed
through formal authority. They called this the **vertical dyad linkage** approach,
and it implied that the proper unit of analysis is the dyad, not the leader.

@graen1995 reviewed twenty-five years of subsequent work and described the
theory's evolution in four stages: discovering differentiated dyads, linking
exchange quality to outcomes, describing how partnerships are built (**leadership
making**), and aggregating dyads to the group and network levels. They argued that
leaders should aim to offer every follower the opportunity to develop a
high-quality relationship rather than accept a fixed in-group and out-group.

### Core logic and propositions

LMX is an application of [social exchange theory](#social-exchange-theory) (Section \@ref(social-exchange-theory)) to the
leader-follower relationship [@cropanzano2005]. Leaders control resources that
followers value: interesting assignments, information, support, discretion, and
advocacy. Followers can offer effort beyond the formal role, loyalty, and
expertise. When early exchanges go well, each side extends more, and the
relationship moves through three stages: **stranger** (formal, contractual
exchange), **acquaintance** (testing and limited reciprocity), and **mature
partnership** (high trust, mutual influence, and obligation) [@graen1995].

- **P1 (Differentiation).** Leaders form relationships of varying quality with
  members of the same unit.
- **P2 (Outcomes).** Higher LMX quality is associated with higher performance,
  satisfaction, commitment, and lower turnover intentions.
- **P3 (Reciprocity).** LMX develops through reciprocal exchange, with early
  interactions and perceived similarity shaping its trajectory.
- **P4 (Team context).** Within a team, large differences in LMX quality can
  harm cooperation and fairness perceptions unless differentiation is seen as
  based on contribution.

### Evidence and extensions

@gerstner1997 meta-analysed the early literature. LMX was associated with
supervisor-rated performance, satisfaction with the supervisor, overall
satisfaction, [organizational commitment](#organizational-commitment), role clarity, and lower turnover
intentions, but not reliably with actual turnover. Two construct issues stood
out: leaders' and members' ratings of the same relationship agreed only
moderately, and correlations were stronger when outcomes were reported by the
same person who rated LMX. @dulebohn2012 extended the synthesis to antecedents:
follower characteristics (competence, conscientiousness), leader characteristics
(expectations of the follower, transformational behaviour), and interpersonal
factors (perceived similarity, liking) all predict LMX quality.

Measurement has evolved with the theory. The seven-item LMX-7 treats exchange
quality as a single dimension [@graen1995], whereas the multidimensional LMX-MDM
separates affect, loyalty, contribution, and professional respect [@liden1998].
More recent work studies **LMX differentiation** at the team level and
**relative LMX**, a member's standing compared with teammates, which links the
theory to [social comparison](#social-comparison-theory) (Section \@ref(social-comparison-theory)).

::: {.debate}
**Is LMX a cause or a consequence of performance?** Leaders form better
relationships with followers who are already competent, and high performers
receive more resources. Cross-sectional correlations between LMX and performance
therefore confound the effect of the relationship with the selection of high
performers into good relationships. The disagreement between leader and member
ratings adds a further problem: if two parties see the same relationship
differently, which view is "the" relationship? Longitudinal designs, dyadic
models that use both reports, and instruments for early relationship formation
are needed to separate the mechanisms [@antonakis2010].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: LMX in team management.** A newly promoted engineering
manager inherits eight engineers. Within weeks, she relies heavily on two senior
engineers for design decisions and status updates, while the others receive
assignments by ticket. LMX theory predicts that the two will become more
committed and influential and that the remaining six may disengage, especially if
they see the split as favouritism. Practical steps drawn from the leadership-making
stage model include offering every team member a stretch assignment early (an
opening move in the exchange), holding regular one-to-one meetings with all
reports, and making the criteria for access to high-visibility work explicit so
that differentiation is seen as earned. Monitoring the *spread* of relationship
quality, not just its average, becomes part of the manager's dashboard.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* LMX quality is positively related to organizational citizenship behaviour,
  and the relationship is mediated by felt obligation.
- *H2.* LMX differentiation within teams is negatively related to team
  coordination when team members perceive differentiation as unfair.
- *H3.* Relative LMX (a member's LMX compared with the team mean) predicts
  self-efficacy beyond the member's absolute LMX.

**Validated scales.** LMX-7 [@graen1995]. LMX-MDM [@liden1998].

**Designs.** Dyadic data from both leaders and members analysed with dyadic or
multilevel models. Longitudinal studies of newly formed dyads. Team-level designs
with polynomial regression for relative standing. Field experiments in leader
training that encourage equal opportunities for exchange.

**Contexts.** New-hire onboarding, matrix organizations, remote teams, sales
territories.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Ignoring reverse causality and same-source bias.** A survey that asks employees
to rate both their relationship with the manager and their own engagement will
almost always find a strong correlation. Use supervisor- or record-based
outcomes, measure LMX before outcomes, and model the possibility that
performance shapes the relationship.
:::

## Transformational Leadership {#transformational-leadership}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Transformational leaders raise followers' motivation and
performance beyond what exchange-based incentives achieve by articulating an
inspiring vision, serving as role models, stimulating new thinking, and attending
to individual needs.

**Origins.** Political science and organizational psychology. @burns1978
distinguished transforming from transactional political leadership. @bass1985
operationalised the distinction for organizations.

**Level of analysis.** Individual leader and followers, with group-level
extensions.

**Key constructs.** Idealised influence (charisma), inspirational motivation,
intellectual stimulation, individualised consideration, contingent reward,
management by exception, laissez-faire leadership.

**Boundary conditions.** Effects are thought to be stronger in uncertain or
crisis conditions and when followers identify with the collective. Measurement
problems limit what current evidence can show (see the debate below).

**Related theories.** [Leader-member exchange](#leader-member-exchange),
[Path-goal theory](#path-goal-theory),
[Social identity theory](#social-identity-theory) (Section \@ref(social-identity-theory)),
[Upper echelons theory](#upper-echelons-theory) (Section \@ref(upper-echelons-theory)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

@burns1978, a political historian, contrasted two kinds of leaders. **Transactional**
leaders exchange one thing for another: jobs for votes, subsidies for
contributions. **Transforming** leaders engage followers so that both are raised
to higher levels of motivation and morality. @bass1985 brought the idea into
organizational psychology and, unlike Burns, treated transformational and
transactional leadership as complementary rather than opposite ends of a single
continuum. A leader can do both, and transformational behaviour *adds* to the
effect of transactional leadership, an idea known as the **augmentation
effect**. Elaborated by Bass and colleagues into what they called the "full range"
model of leadership, this framework became the most researched approach to
leadership of the following three decades.

### Core logic and propositions

The full-range model distinguishes three families of behaviour
(Table \@ref(tab:tab-wl-leadership) compares them with the other leadership
theories in this chapter):

- **Transformational**: *idealised influence* (acting as a role model who
  inspires trust and identification), *inspirational motivation* (articulating an
  appealing vision), *intellectual stimulation* (challenging assumptions and
  encouraging creativity), and *individualised consideration* (coaching and
  attending to each follower's needs).
- **Transactional**: *contingent reward* (clarifying expectations and rewarding
  their achievement) and *management by exception* (monitoring and correcting
  deviations, either actively or passively).
- **Laissez-faire**: the avoidance of leadership responsibilities.

The theory's central proposition is that transformational behaviours change
followers' values, self-concepts, and identification with the collective, so that
they pursue collective goals for intrinsic reasons rather than for rewards alone.

```{r tab-wl-leadership}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Feature, ~`Leader-member exchange`, ~`Transformational leadership`, ~`Path-goal theory`,
  "Focal unit", "Leader-follower dyad", "Leader and followers as a group", "Leader, follower, and task",
  "Core mechanism", "Reciprocal social exchange", "Identification and value change", "Expectancy: clarifying paths and raising valences",
  "Key behaviours", "Offering latitude, support, and challenging assignments", "Vision, role modelling, stimulation, consideration", "Directive, supportive, participative, achievement-oriented",
  "Contingency view", "Weak: quality varies by relationship", "Weak: broadly effective", "Strong: best behaviour depends on task and follower",
  "Main measure", "LMX-7, LMX-MDM", "Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire", "Leader behaviour scales",
  "Main critique", "Reverse causality, rater disagreement", "Conflates behaviour with effects", "Mixed tests, many untested propositions"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Three leadership theories compared.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The quantitative evidence is large. @judge2004 meta-analysed studies of the full
range model and found that transformational leadership was strongly related to
follower satisfaction, motivation, and rated leader effectiveness. Contingent
reward, a transactional behaviour, showed overall validities of a similar size and
was in some settings as predictive as transformational leadership, while
laissez-faire leadership was negatively related to outcomes. The authors also found
that the relative validity of the dimensions differed across settings and that
transformational and contingent reward leadership were highly correlated, which
made their unique effects hard to separate.

Experimental evidence is thinner but exists. In a small field experiment,
@barling1996 trained bank branch managers in transformational leadership and
found improvements in subordinates' perceptions of their managers, in
subordinates' organizational commitment, and in branch-level financial outcomes
compared with an untrained control group. The study is often cited because it
combines random assignment with objective outcomes, but its sample was small.

::: {.debate}
**Back to the drawing board?** @vanknippenberg2013 published a sweeping critique of
charismatic-transformational leadership research. They argued, first, that the
construct lacks an independent definition: it is defined largely by its effects
(followers who are inspired and perform beyond expectations), which makes the
link between leadership and outcomes partly tautological. Second, the theory does
not explain why these four particular dimensions belong together or how each
produces its effects. Third, the dominant measures, especially the Multifactor
Leadership Questionnaire, ask followers to rate behaviours in terms that already
include positive outcomes, and the proposed dimensional structure is often not
reproduced empirically. They recommended abandoning the umbrella construct and
studying specific, well-defined leader behaviours and their mechanisms. A related
methodological critique notes that follower ratings of leadership are endogenous
to performance, liking, and attributions, so most observational estimates are
biased [@antonakis2010]. Defenders point to experimental studies like
@barling1996 and argue that refinement, not abandonment, is the appropriate
response. The debate is not settled, but it has raised the standard of evidence
expected of leadership research.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Leadership development programmes.** Transformational leadership is the
intellectual backbone of many corporate leadership development curricula, which
teach managers to communicate a vision, coach individuals, and encourage
challenge to the status quo. The evidence suggests three design principles. First,
do not neglect transactional basics: clear goals and contingent recognition are
consistently effective [@judge2004]. Second, evaluate programmes with outcomes
that are not rated by the same followers who rate the leader, as
@barling1996 did with branch financial data. Third, teach specific behaviours
(how to give developmental feedback, how to frame change around shared values)
rather than an abstract "inspirational style", in line with
@vanknippenberg2013.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Leaders' intellectual stimulation is positively related to team
  creativity, and the relationship is mediated by psychological safety.
- *H2.* Contingent reward leadership explains variance in follower performance
  beyond transformational leadership in routine production settings.
- *H3.* Training in vision communication increases objectively measured unit
  performance relative to a control group.

**Validated scales.** The Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire, developed from
@bass1985, remains the most common instrument, but users should report evidence
on its factor structure in their sample and consider behaviour-specific
alternatives.

**Designs.** Randomised leadership training with objective outcomes. Laboratory
experiments that manipulate a specific leader behaviour (for example, a vision
speech). Designs that address endogeneity, such as instrumental variables or
exogenous leader turnover [@antonakis2010].

**Contexts.** Organizational change and turnaround, start-ups, military and
public-service organizations, healthcare teams.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Measuring leadership with outcomes.** Items such as "my leader motivates me to
do more than I expected" fold the dependent variable into the independent
variable. Use behaviour-specific measures, separate sources, and designs that
can support causal claims before concluding that a leader's style caused
performance.
:::

## Path-Goal Theory {#path-goal-theory}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Effective leaders increase followers' motivation by clarifying the
paths to work goals, removing obstacles, and making goal attainment more
rewarding. The behaviour that does this best depends on the task and the
follower.

**Origins.** Organizational psychology. @house1971, reformulated in
@house1996.

**Level of analysis.** Leader-follower dyad and work group.

**Key constructs.** Directive, supportive, participative, and achievement-oriented
leader behaviour, task structure, follower ability, locus of control,
expectancies, valences.

**Boundary conditions.** Leader behaviour matters only where the situation does not
already provide clarity and rewards, that is, where there are few
**substitutes for leadership** [@kerr1978].

**Related theories.** [Expectancy theory](#expectancy-theory) (Section \@ref(expectancy-theory)),
[Transformational leadership](#transformational-leadership),
[Goal-setting theory](#goal-setting-theory) (Section \@ref(goal-setting-theory)).
:::

@house1971 built path-goal theory directly on [expectancy theory](#expectancy-theory) (Section \@ref(expectancy-theory))
[@vroom1964]. Followers are motivated when they believe effort leads to
performance and performance leads to valued rewards. The leader's job is to
strengthen both links: clarify what effective performance requires, remove
roadblocks, provide support, and tie rewards to goal attainment. Because these
needs vary, the theory is explicitly **contingent**. Directive leadership helps
when tasks are ambiguous and followers inexperienced, but is redundant or even
irritating when tasks are routine and well understood. Supportive leadership
helps most when tasks are stressful, boring, or dangerous. Participative
leadership suits followers who want control, and achievement-oriented leadership
suits complex tasks where high standards and confidence in followers raise
expectancies (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wl-pathgoal)).

```{r fig-wl-pathgoal, fig.cap = "Path-goal theory. Leader behaviour affects follower expectancies and valences, which drive motivation and performance. Task and follower characteristics determine which behaviour is effective. Adapted from House (1971, 1996)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  L [label = "Leader behaviour\\n(directive, supportive,\\nparticipative,\\nachievement-oriented)", %s]
  X [label = "Follower expectancies\\nand valences\\n(path clarity, rewards)", %s]
  M [label = "Motivation\\nSatisfaction\\nPerformance", %s]
  T [label = "Task characteristics\\n(structure, stress)", %s]
  F [label = "Follower characteristics\\n(ability, locus of control)", %s]
  L -> X -> M
  T -> X [style = dashed]
  F -> X [style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator, node_moderator))
```

The evidence is mixed. A meta-analysis by @wofford1993 found support for some
propositions and not for others, and noted that many tests used weak designs and
measures. @house1996 acknowledged these limitations and reformulated the theory
around a broader set of leader behaviours, including work facilitation,
interaction facilitation, group-oriented decision processes, representation and
networking, and value-based behaviour, while retaining the core idea that leaders
compensate for what the environment does not provide. A related line of work on
**substitutes for leadership** argued that professional training, intrinsically
satisfying tasks, and formalised procedures can make some leader behaviours
unnecessary [@kerr1978]. Path-goal theory's lasting contribution is less any single
prediction than the principle that leadership style should be matched to the
motivational deficits of a specific situation.

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: one manager, two teams.** A regional operations manager
oversees a newly formed analytics team working on ill-defined problems and a
mature payroll team running a stable, highly regulated process. Path-goal theory
predicts that directive behaviour (clear problem definitions, milestones, and
methods) will raise the analytics team's expectancies, while the same behaviour
would be redundant for payroll. The payroll team, facing repetitive work and
deadline stress at month end, benefits more from supportive behaviour and from
removing obstacles such as late data from other departments. The prescription is
not a single best style but a deliberate diagnosis of what each team lacks.
:::

## Psychological Contract Theory {#psychological-contract}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Employees hold beliefs about the reciprocal promises that bind them
and their employer. When they perceive that the organization has broken those
promises, they react with feelings of violation and reduced trust, commitment,
and effort, even if no written agreement was breached.

**Origins.** Organizational behaviour. @rousseau1989 reconceptualised the
psychological contract as an individual-level belief, extended in @rousseau1995.
@robinson1994 and @morrison1997 developed the theory of breach and violation.

**Level of analysis.** Individual employee, in relation to the organization and its
agents.

**Key constructs.** Perceived promises, transactional and relational contracts,
breach, violation, reneging, incongruence.

**Boundary conditions.** Applies where employment involves promises that are
implicit, long-term, or incompletely specified. Contract content varies with
career stage, labour market, and national employment norms.

**Related theories.** [Social exchange theory](#social-exchange-theory) (Section \@ref(social-exchange-theory)),
[Organizational justice](#organizational-justice),
[Organizational commitment](#organizational-commitment).
:::

### Core logic

Earlier writers used "psychological contract" loosely to describe unwritten
expectations between employees and employers. @rousseau1989 gave the concept a
precise meaning: an individual's **belief** about the terms of a reciprocal
exchange with another party, grounded in a perceived **promise**. Because it is a
belief, two employees in the same job can hold different contracts, and the
organization, which consists of many agents (recruiters, managers, HR policies),
cannot simply read off what it has promised. @rousseau1995 distinguished
**transactional** contracts, which are specific, short-term, and largely monetary,
from **relational** contracts, which are open-ended and include loyalty, support,
and development. Later typologies add balanced and transitional forms (Table \@ref(tab:tab-wl-contract)).

```{r tab-wl-contract}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Feature, ~`Transactional contract`, ~`Relational contract`,
  "Time frame", "Short-term, specified duration", "Open-ended, long-term",
  "Content", "Pay for defined performance", "Pay plus loyalty, development, security",
  "Specificity", "Explicit and narrow", "Implicit and broad",
  "Typical setting", "Contract and gig work, fixed-term projects", "Career employment, internal labour markets",
  "Typical reaction to breach", "Renegotiation or exit", "Felt betrayal, withdrawal of discretionary effort",
  "Employer lever", "Clear terms and prompt payment", "Consistent signals from managers and policies"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Transactional and relational psychological contracts, following Rousseau (1995).")
```

@morrison1997 separated two reactions that earlier work had merged. **Breach** is
the cognitive perception that the organization has failed to fulfil one or more
obligations. **Violation** is the emotional experience of anger and betrayal that
may follow. Breach can arise from **reneging**, when agents knowingly fail to keep
a promise, or from **incongruence**, when the two parties understood the promise
differently. Whether breach turns into violation depends on how the employee
interprets it, especially on attributions of intent and perceptions of fairness.

### Evidence

The landmark longitudinal study by @robinson1994 surveyed graduates of a master
of business administration programme when they took up new jobs and again two
years later. More than half reported that their
employer had violated the psychological contract, which led the authors to
describe violation as the norm rather than the exception. Violation was associated
with lower trust, satisfaction, and intentions to remain. A follow-up longitudinal
study confirmed that breach and violation are distinct, and that the step from one
to the other depends on attributions of reneging and perceived unfairness
[@robinson2000]. The meta-analysis by @zhao2007 found that breach is related to
feelings of violation and mistrust, to lower job satisfaction and organizational
commitment, to higher turnover intentions, and to reduced citizenship behaviour
and in-role performance, with affective reactions mediating many of these links.

::: {.debate}
**Whose contract?** Because the psychological contract exists in the employee's
mind, critics question whether "contract" is the right metaphor: a contract
normally requires mutual agreement, and the organization is not a single party
that can hold beliefs. Measurement adds a second problem. Many studies ask
employees directly how well promises have been fulfilled, which mixes perceived
promises, perceived delivery, and evaluation in a single item. Designs that
measure promises at entry and fulfilment later, or that compare employee and
manager views, are more informative.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: return-to-office policies as contract change.** A
software firm hired many employees during a period when remote work was described
in recruiting conversations as permanent. Two years later, it mandates four office
days per week. Legally, nothing has been breached, since the employment contracts
never mentioned location. Psychological contract theory predicts that employees
who perceived a promise will experience breach, and those who attribute it to
reneging will experience violation and withdraw discretionary effort or leave.
The theory suggests three mitigations: acknowledge the change explicitly as a
change, explain the reasons (to shift attributions from reneging to necessity),
and offer something in exchange, such as transition time or flexible days, so that
the reciprocal balance is restored.
:::

## Organizational Justice {#organizational-justice}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Employees evaluate not only what they receive (distributive
justice) but also how decisions are made (procedural justice) and how they are
treated and informed (interactional justice). Each form of fairness has distinct
effects on attitudes and behaviour.

**Origins.** Social psychology and organizational behaviour.
[Equity theory](#equity-theory) (Section \@ref(equity-theory)) [@adams1965], procedural justice in legal settings
[@thibaut1975], allocation procedures [@leventhal1980], and interactional justice
[@bies1986]. Integrated by @colquitt2001a and @colquitt2001.

**Level of analysis.** Individual perceptions of organizational decisions, with
extensions to team justice climate.

**Key constructs.** Distributive, procedural, interpersonal, and informational
justice, voice, fair process effect.

**Boundary conditions.** The weight of procedural justice is greatest when outcomes
are unfavourable or uncertain. Reactions to voice vary with cultural values such
as power distance [@brockner2001b].

**Related theories.** [Equity theory](#equity-theory) (Section \@ref(equity-theory)),
[Psychological contract](#psychological-contract),
[Social exchange theory](#social-exchange-theory) (Section \@ref(social-exchange-theory)),
[Leader-member exchange](#leader-member-exchange).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Justice research began with outcomes. [Equity theory](#equity-theory) (Section \@ref(equity-theory)) proposed
that people compare their ratio of outcomes to inputs with that of others and
feel distress when the ratios differ [@adams1965]. This is **distributive
justice**. @thibaut1975 shifted attention to process. Studying legal dispute
resolution, they found that people's satisfaction depended heavily on **process
control**, the opportunity to present their case, even when they had no control
over the final decision. This became known as the **voice** effect. @leventhal1980
extended procedural justice to organizational allocation decisions and proposed six
rules that make procedures fair. @bies1986 added **interactional justice**: the
quality of interpersonal treatment people receive when procedures are enacted,
including truthfulness, justification, respect, and propriety.

### Core logic and propositions

Table \@ref(tab:tab-wl-justice) summarises the four dimensions that most
researchers now use, following the construct validation by @colquitt2001a, which
showed that separating interactional justice into interpersonal and informational
components fit the data better than three-factor alternatives.

```{r tab-wl-justice}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Dimension, ~`Focal question`, ~`Fairness criteria`, ~`Key source`,
  "Distributive", "Are outcomes fair given contributions?", "Equity (also equality or need in some settings)", "Adams (1965)",
  "Procedural", "Is the decision process fair?", "Voice, consistency, bias suppression, accuracy, correctability, representation, ethicality", "Thibaut & Walker (1975), Leventhal (1980)",
  "Interpersonal", "Was I treated with dignity and respect?", "Respect, propriety", "Bies & Moag (1986)",
  "Informational", "Was the decision explained truthfully and adequately?", "Truthfulness, justification, timeliness", "Bies & Moag (1986)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Four dimensions of organizational justice, following Colquitt (2001).")
```

The theory's main propositions are:

- **P1 (Distinctiveness).** The justice dimensions are related but distinct, and
  each explains unique variance in outcomes [@colquitt2001].
- **P2 (Targets).** Procedural justice is most strongly tied to evaluations of the
  organization and its systems, while interpersonal and informational justice are
  most strongly tied to evaluations of the decision agent, typically the
  supervisor.
- **P3 (Fair process effect).** Fair procedures and treatment soften negative
  reactions to unfavourable outcomes. Procedural justice matters most when
  outcomes are poor [@brockner1996].
- **P4 (Behaviour).** Perceived injustice leads to withdrawal, reduced citizenship,
  and retaliation, while justice fosters trust, commitment, and cooperation.

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-wl-fairprocess) sketches the interaction behind P3.

```{r fig-wl-fairprocess, fig.cap = "Stylised fair process effect. When outcomes are favourable, procedures matter little. When outcomes are unfavourable, fair procedures and treatment greatly reduce negative reactions. Pattern consistent with the interaction reviewed by Brockner and Wiesenfeld (1996). Not empirical data.", fig.height = 3.8}
fp <- tibble::tribble(
  ~outcome, ~process, ~support,
  "Unfavourable outcome", "Low procedural fairness", 2.0,
  "Unfavourable outcome", "High procedural fairness", 4.1,
  "Favourable outcome", "Low procedural fairness", 5.3,
  "Favourable outcome", "High procedural fairness", 5.8
) |>
  mutate(outcome = factor(outcome, levels = c("Unfavourable outcome", "Favourable outcome")))
ggplot(fp, aes(outcome, support, colour = process, group = process)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.92, xend = 0.92, y = 2.1, yend = 4.0,
           colour = ink[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.4,
           arrow = grid::arrow(ends = "both", length = grid::unit(0.08, "inches"))) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.88, y = 3.05, label = "Large gap:\nprocess matters\nmost here",
           hjust = 1, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("High procedural fairness" = pal[["blue"]], "Low procedural fairness" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1, 7), breaks = 1:7) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Support for the decision (1-7)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Procedural fairness matters most when outcomes are bad",
       caption = "Stylised values chosen to illustrate the outcome x procedure interaction.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The meta-analysis by @colquitt2001 integrated twenty-five years of research. It
found that the justice dimensions are strongly correlated but distinguishable,
that procedural justice predicts a wide range of attitudes and behaviours, and that
interpersonal and informational justice add explanatory power beyond procedural
and distributive justice. Two field studies became classics. In a manufacturing
company that imposed a temporary pay cut, @greenberg1990 found that employee theft
rose in the affected plants, and that it rose much less in the plant where
management explained the cut thoroughly and with expressed regret. In a study of
terminated employees, @lind2000 found that how fairly people felt they had been
treated at the time of termination was a strong predictor of whether they
filed wrongful-termination claims. Both studies show that the *manner* of an
unfavourable decision has economic consequences.

::: {.debate}
**How many dimensions, and is fairness one judgment?** The four-factor structure
is well supported psychometrically, but the dimensions are highly correlated and
often have similar effects. Some researchers therefore argue for an **overall
justice** judgment that people form quickly and then use as a heuristic, with the
specific dimensions as its inputs. A second debate concerns the boundary between
interactional and procedural justice: if a respectful explanation is part of the
procedure, is it a separate dimension? Cultural research adds a third: the voice
effect is weaker in high power-distance settings, where employees expect less say
in decisions [@brockner2001b].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Layoffs and procedural justice.** Layoffs are the clearest test of the fair
process effect: the outcome is unfavourable by definition, for victims and often
for survivors. The research above suggests a practical checklist. Use consistent,
pre-announced criteria (consistency and bias suppression). Give employees a way
to correct errors in the data used for selection (correctability). Explain the
business reasons candidly and early (informational justice). Deliver the news in
person, privately, and with respect, never by mass e-mail (interpersonal justice).
Provide fair severance and outplacement support (distributive justice). The
evidence that poor treatment at termination predicts legal claims [@lind2000] and
that explanations reduce retaliation [@greenberg1990] means these steps reduce
legal and operational risk as well as human cost. Survivors watch how departing
colleagues are treated and update their own trust and commitment accordingly
[@brockner1996].
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Informational justice during an organizational change is positively
  related to change acceptance, and the effect is stronger when the change is
  unfavourable to the employee.
- *H2.* Interpersonal justice from the supervisor predicts supervisor-directed
  citizenship behaviour more strongly than procedural justice does.
- *H3.* Team justice climate moderates the relationship between individual
  justice perceptions and team commitment.

**Validated scales.** Colquitt's four-dimension organizational justice measure
[@colquitt2001a].

**Designs.** Vignette and laboratory experiments manipulating outcome and process
independently. Field quasi-experiments around layoffs, pay changes, or appraisal
system redesign. Multilevel designs for justice climate. Archival data on
grievances and legal claims.

**Contexts.** Performance appraisal, pay decisions, downsizing, algorithmic
management, promotion systems.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Treating fairness as an outcome only.** Many organizations evaluate decisions
solely by asking whether outcomes are defensible. Justice research shows that
process and treatment often matter as much, especially when the outcome is bad.
In research, the parallel mistake is to measure a single global fairness item
and attribute effects to a specific dimension.
:::

## Organizational Commitment {#organizational-commitment}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Commitment to an organization is a psychological state with three
components: a desire to stay (affective commitment), a perceived need to stay
because of the costs of leaving (continuance commitment), and a felt obligation to
stay (normative commitment). Each has different antecedents and consequences.

**Origins.** Organizational psychology. @meyer1991, with measures in
@allen1990.

**Level of analysis.** Individual employee.

**Key constructs.** Affective, continuance, and normative commitment, commitment
profiles, side bets, perceived alternatives.

**Boundary conditions.** Developed in North American samples with conventional
employment. Normative commitment may operate differently in more collectivist
cultures.

**Related theories.** [Psychological contract](#psychological-contract),
[Social identity theory](#social-identity-theory) (Section \@ref(social-identity-theory)),
[Escalation of commitment](#escalation-of-commitment) (Section \@ref(escalation-of-commitment)).
:::

Earlier research on commitment had followed separate threads: some scholars saw
commitment as emotional attachment, others as the accumulation of investments
(side bets) that would be lost on leaving, and still others as a moral duty.
@meyer1991 argued that these were not competing definitions but distinct
**components** of commitment that can coexist in the same person in different
strengths. All three tie an employee to the organization, but they do so for
different reasons and should therefore have different effects on behaviour beyond
staying (Table \@ref(tab:tab-wl-commitment)).

```{r tab-wl-commitment}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Component, ~Mindset, ~`Typical antecedents`, ~`Relation to performance and citizenship`,
  "Affective", "I want to stay", "Supportive leadership, justice, meaningful work", "Positive",
  "Continuance", "I need to stay", "Investments that would be lost, few alternatives", "Weak or negative",
  "Normative", "I ought to stay", "Socialization, reciprocity for benefits received", "Positive, weaker than affective"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "The three-component model of organizational commitment, following Meyer and Allen (1991) and Meyer et al. (2002).")
```

The meta-analysis by @meyer2002 supported this differentiation. All three
components were negatively related to turnover intentions and turnover. Affective
commitment had the strongest and most favourable correlations with attendance,
